sections.h2: Selling a house in Eau Claire
sections.html:
The Eau Claire and Chippewa rivers meet in Eau Claire, the seat of Eau Claire County, which had an estimated 72,465 residents in July 2025 (4.4% above 2020). With more renters than owners, many sales involve tenants, small apartment buildings or houses near the university. Because part of the city falls in Chippewa County, parcels there answer to that county's Register of Deeds and treasurer, so verify yours.

Agent listing, owner sale or cash buyer: the same four items drive the timeline. They are city permit records, the assessment and tax calendar, the seller disclosure report and the deed recording at the county.

Owners occupy only a little over half of Eau Claire homes, which makes rentals a big slice of the market. Older neighborhoods such as Randall Park, Third Ward and the Emery Street Bungalow district contribute bungalows and big lumber-era houses to resale.

Buyers ask about schools. The Eau Claire Area School District office can tell you which school a given address feeds, which is especially worth asking for parcels on the city's edge that may belong to a different district.

sections.h2: Assessment, appeals and the tax calendar
sections.html:
January 1 is Eau Claire's assessment date. A tax bill can be paid whole by January 31, or in halves on January 31 and July 31. Assessment change notices normally come between late April and late May, and the Board of Review meets within 45 days of the fourth Monday in April.

  • Start with an assessor. The city calls that informal conversation the way to learn how your value was figured.
  • A Board decision you dislike can go to the Department of Revenue within 20 days of receipt, with a $100 fee, provided the disputed value is $1 million or less.
  • The court route has a 90-day limit from the Board's adjournment, and the judge works from the record of your hearing.

Reach the assessor at 715-839-4926, and use the city's Beacon tool to search property records. A full-year tax bill gets prorated at closing, with the title company showing who pays what. The Eau Claire County treasurer can tell you where any unpaid bill on the parcel stands.

Plan review, permits and inspections for building, heating, air conditioning, electrical and plumbing work come from Inspection Services, which also enforces floodplain, zoning, upkeep and land use ordinances. Use the Evolve portal or the phone for requests, since individual inspectors do not take them by email.

Short-term rentals fall under their own rules, which affect how a future owner can use the house. Chapter 5.66 created the Short-Term Rental License.

  • First comes a Tourist Rooming House license, issued through the combined city and county Health Department at 715-839-4718.
  • Second is city review by Planning and Zoning at 715-839-4914, which asks for a parking count, a building plan and a trash container sketch.
  • The fee is $700 for the first review and $300 to renew each year, on a June 30 to June 30 cycle.

If the house has been a short-term rental, confirm the license with Planning before listing. A buyer who wants to continue the use will ask.

The Eau Claire County Register of Deeds takes deeds, mortgages, satisfactions, plats and certified survey maps. Paper filers must now include a postage-paid return envelope, a rule in place since January 1, 2025. The county's land records page carries forms, the electronic transfer return, a recording checklist and the fee schedule, and the office answers email at rod@eauclairecounty.gov.

Wis. Stat. 77.22 makes the grantor pay 30 cents per $100 of value, which the register collects when the deed comes in. The register is not responsible for verifying the value reported. When the transfer is a gift or has only nominal consideration, Wis. Stat. 77.21 uses the estimated open-market price, a point that matters when a relative buys at a discount.

Sellers of one-to-four-unit property deliver a finished condition report to the buyer within 10 days of an accepted contract (Chapter 709). Condominium sellers add an addendum with condominium information at the same time. A report that never arrives lets the buyer rescind within two business days after the 10 days end, with deposits returned.

The exception is narrow: personal representatives, trustees, conservators and court-supervised fiduciaries who never lived in the house. A regular owner, a landlord included, completes the report.

A landlord should settle early whether the buyer gets the property occupied. Gather the lease and rent roll, warn the tenant before showings, and check any short-term rental license. Investors will want those papers, while a buyer who plans to move in will want a date for delivery empty.

Permit records matter as much as for an owner-occupied house, and a buyer's lender or inspector may ask for them. Ask Inspection Services about open work, and ask the Eau Claire County treasurer about the tax balance on each parcel you are selling.

Listing is a good route when the house shows well and you can manage showings and a lender's schedule. Cash fits deferred repairs, a tenant in place, a probate timeline or a payoff date.

Put every offer through a net sheet that lists the loan payoff, the $3 per $1,000 transfer fee, recording, prorated tax and repair credits. That way offers are compared on proceeds, not on the price alone. Ask for each figure in writing and keep the sheet with your closing file.

1. Pull permit and inspection records from Inspection Services.
  2. Learn which county, Eau Claire or Chippewa, applies to your parcel.
  3. Get the tax status from the county treasurer and a proration estimate from the title company.
  4. Prepare the condition report, plus the condominium addendum if it applies.
  5. Download the electronic transfer return and recording checklist from the land records page.

Those five items cover almost everything that delays an Eau Claire closing. If you are selling for a family member or an estate, check whether the fiduciary exception applies before you start the condition report, and ask the title company who will prepare the deed. When the buyer is paying cash, the same list still applies, though the lender's timeline drops out. Keep copies of every confirmation, because the title company will want the tax status, permit record and report delivery date in one file.

faqs.q: Which office records an Eau Claire deed?
faqs.a: The Eau Claire County Register of Deeds. Include a postage-paid return envelope for paper documents, and ask for the current filing fee schedule before you submit.

faqs.q: What are the Eau Claire property tax due dates?
faqs.a: January 31 for a full payment, or two installments on January 31 and July 31. The assessment date is January 1.

faqs.q: What transfer fee does an Eau Claire seller pay?
faqs.a: 30 cents per $100 of value, under Wis. Stat. 77.22.

faqs.q: Is a license needed for a short-term rental in Eau Claire?
faqs.a: Yes. You need a Tourist Rooming House license from the Health Department and a city Short-Term Rental License, with a $700 initial review fee and a $300 annual renewal.

faqs.q: Can I appeal after the Eau Claire Board of Review?
faqs.a: Yes. Appeal to the Wisconsin Department of Revenue within 20 days of the decision for a $100 filing fee, or go to circuit court within 90 days after the Board adjourns.
